t: one who injures his fellow. Who inflicted a wound on his body (for the prohibition of injuring see below 5:1).
is liable to pay him five things. The payment relates to several possible components of an injury, and the injurer may be liable for only some of these five (as below 2:1).
damage. Payment for the permanent harm to the injured person's body.
and pain. Compensation for pain.
and loss of time. Payment for loss of working days.
and shame. Payment for having embarrassed him.

they are paid from the best of his property. When collecting from land, one collects from the finest (but if the damager has movable property one collects from it of any kind - see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 8:10, below 7:16).
like the law of all damagers. See Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:2.
how is damage assessed. How the damage is estimated.
how much he was worth and how much he is worth now. How much such a slave was worth before the amputation and how much he is worth now.

as it is said, "eye for eye". Scripture continues: "tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise" (Exodus 21:24-25), and from it we learn that the injurer must pay the value of what he damaged, as explained shortly.
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
it is payment of money. And not that he is injured as he injured his fellow.
but he deserves to be deprived of a limb, etc.. It was fitting that a blemish be inflicted on him as he inflicted on his fellow, and the payment is a substitute for this.
that you shall not have pity regarding the payments. And the meaning of the verse is not that you shall not have pity in depriving him of a limb or injuring him as he did to his fellow.

and from where, etc.. Although we already learned from another derivation that one pays money for injuries (above, halakhah 3), one might have thought that there is a choice between payment of money and an actual injury, and therefore this derivation was brought (see Lechem Mishneh, Me'irat Einayim).

and if a man strikes his fellow with a stone, etc.. And just as for this blow that causes a bruise it says that he pays only money, so in the verse "bruise for bruise" the meaning is payment of money.

although these matters appear to be from the subject of the Written Torah, all of them are explained from the mouth of Moses from Mount Sinai, etc.. The law that a person who injures his fellow pays him money and is not injured can be learned from the meaning of the verses themselves as explained above, and yet it was also told to Moses at Sinai explicitly and transmitted by tradition to the Sages, and so the courts in practice have conducted themselves from the days of Moses until today.
and from where do we learn that one who damages his fellow is liable for pain separately. As a payment separate from the payment of damage.

for it is said regarding the rapist, "because he has afflicted her". From this verse they learned that besides the other payments the rapist must pay the girl, he also pays for the pain he caused her when he had relations with her against her will (see Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 2:1).
as it is said, etc.. Regarding one who strikes his fellow and he fell ill.

and you shall cut off her hand: included in this law is the fine of the one who shames. Although from this verse they learned that one may injure the assailant when there is concern for a life (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 1:7-8), they also learned from it the obligation to pay money in a case of shame (see Even HaAzel).

he is not liable for shame unless he intended. That he intended the act that caused the shame, unlike the other payments, for which he is liable even when he did not intend to do the act (see below, halakhah 12).
a person is always forewarned. A person is always warned against causing damage.

whether unintentional or deliberate, etc.. This is regarding payment of damage, which he must pay in every case of damaging. But regarding the other four payments there is a difference: if he damaged unintentionally he is exempt from shame and liable for pain, healing and loss of time, and if he was compelled he is exempt from all four payments and liable only for damage (see below, halakhot 12, 15; and see below, halakhah 16, that this rule applies in the domain of the damaged party, but in other domains the law differs).
damaged his fellow's property. See below 6:1.
he pays from the best of his property. As above, halakhah 1.
two who slept as one. Who went to sleep at the same time.
the one who came last is the forewarned one. He is the one who was negligent by coming after the first was already asleep, and therefore the sleeper who damaged him is exempt.
and likewise if he placed a vessel beside the sleeper and the sleeper broke it, the sleeper is exempt. The sleeper is exempt from paying for breaking the vessel.

one who fell from a roof in an ordinary wind and damaged is liable for four things. Since he should have been careful of an ordinary wind, he is not considered compelled but unintentional, and is liable for the four payments.
and exempt from shame. Because he did not intend the act that caused the shame.
fell in an unusual wind, he is liable for damage only and exempt from four things. Because he is compelled he is liable only for damage and exempt from the other payments.
and if he turned over. While falling he turned over intending to fall on his fellow, so as not to be dashed against the ground, and not intending to shame him.
and they divide among themselves. They divide the payment among themselves.
and shamed the adult. Without intent.

he gives the adult the value of the minor's shame. Since shame depends on intent, he pays according to the shame of the one he intended to shame (for one who shames a minor or a slave is not like one who shames an adult or a free man, as below 3:4).
whether he never recognized it. He was not aware that it was in his lap.
and it fell. Without his knowledge.
he is liable for damage only and exempt from four things. For he is considered compelled and is liable only for damage (as above, halakhah 12).
he intended to throw two, etc.. He intended to throw the stone a distance of two cubits, but contrary to his intention threw it farther and caused damage; in this case too he is considered compelled.
and the homeowner injured him. Intentionally.
but if the one who entered was injured by the homeowner. The homeowner injured him unintentionally.
the homeowner is exempt. For there is no liability for unintentional damage in the damager's own domain.

and if the homeowner was injured by him, he is liable, because he entered without permission. For a person who damages inside the domain of the injured party is liable even if unintentional or compelled.
both were with permission. For example, the homeowner gave the damager permission to enter, or they were in the public domain where both have permission to walk.
or both without permission. For example, they entered another person's courtyard without his permission.
and they injured each other, both are exempt. For liability for unintentional damage applies only if he entered the injured party's domain without permission (compare below 6:1-3).
and flew off. Was scattered.
or who chopped in a private domain. Even if it is his own.

or one who enters a carpenter's shop, whether with permission or without permission, he is liable. Since it is customary to enter a shop even without permission, the carpenter should have been careful not to damage.
in all these he is liable for four things. For he is considered negligent in these cases.
and exempt from shame. For he did not intend to damage (as above 5:10).

just as we assess for death. To hold a person liable for murder we assess the object with which he struck, the place of the blow, the strength of the killer and the strength of the person killed, and he is not liable unless all of these were enough to kill (for the various assessments see Hilchot Rotze'ach chapter 3).
with a small pebble. Several small stones.
and wounded him with a wound. Inflicted a wound on him.
spat. Spat.
on his fellow's body. But if he spat on his clothes he is exempt (see below 3:5).
and the injurer says: it was not enough to damage, and I am like one compelled. I did not imagine that an object like this would cause damage.

the injured party swears and takes, as will be explained. Below 5:4. That in a case where there is no doubt about the event itself but only about its details, the injured party swears and takes, contrary to the usual rule that the burden of proof is on the one who claims from his fellow.
iron has no assessment. There is no need to assess it, and one who injures with it is liable in every case.
and received it. It struck his head.

as it is said, "and he finds his fellow". This verse was said regarding the woodcutter who killed unintentionally, who in this case does not go into exile because the victim brought it on himself by sticking out his head (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 6:9), and the same applies to an injurer, who in this case is exempt from the payments.
wound. Injury.
who blinded. Blinded.
and it swelled and will in the end return. It swelled and will eventually return to its former state.
and it weakened and will in the end live. It became ill and will eventually recover.
he pays four. For liability for payment of damage applies only for an injury that does not return to normal.
he pays three. He does not pay damage, since the swelling will eventually heal, and he does not pay loss of time, because he is not prevented from working.
struck him. An injury that returns to normal.
in a place that is not seen. Where it is customary to cover it with clothing, and there is no shame here.
struck him with a cloth in his hand or with a document. And there is no pain in this blow, only shame.
burned him. Inflicted a burn on him.
with a skewer or a nail. Heated red-hot.
in a place that does not form a bruise. And there is no permanent damage here and no medical expenses.
and does not prevent work. And there is no loss of time here.
applied a drug to him and changed the appearance of his skin. He rubbed his skin with ointment and as a result a discoloration formed.
confined him in a room. And he could not engage in his work.
gives him only the value of his shame. For being shaved is a shame.
because it will eventually return. And therefore he does not pay the other payments.
shaved him with a drug. Removed his hair with a caustic substance.
that he burned. Inflicted a burn on him.
for damage. For taking the hair (Me'iri, Bava Kamma 85b).
and pain. For the pain caused to him by the drug or the burn.
and healing. Of the head.
the locks of his head. The strands of his hair.
and he is found idle from this work. Specifically if this was his work before; but if it was not his work, the loss of time is assessed in the usual way (as below, halakhah 11, Me'irat Einayim).
even if he knocked out his tooth. And there is no cure for the tooth itself.
the flesh of the teeth needs healing. And because of the need to heal the gums he pays healing and loss of time.
even if he diminished the skin of his flesh by a hair's breadth. Although this is not a missing limb.
for skin does not return. To be as it was, and the scar reduces the value of a slave sold in the market, and there is damage here.
and tore the skin and drew blood from it. For such a tear does not heal again without leaving a mark.
he is exempt by human law. For fear and panic are within the control of the injured party, and therefore it is as if he damaged himself (see Talmud Bava Kamma 91a).

and liable by the laws of Heaven. For although the court cannot hold him liable, nevertheless morally he is responsible for what happened and should pay (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 2:19 and the rulings and opinions there).
and shouted into his ear. Shouted into his ear.

seized him and shouted into his ear and deafened him, or touched him and pushed him, etc.. For in these cases it was impossible for the injured party to flee and avoid the fright (Yad Peshutah, based on Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 8:2).
for we do not recognize the matter, lest he deceive. One cannot know immediately whether he really became deaf or blind, and he can deceive in the matter.
how much is the pain. How is pain assessed.

there is a person who is very delicate and refined and wealthy, etc.. According to the sensitivity and wealth of the injured party, we estimate how much money he would be willing to accept to endure this pain (Mishnah Bava Kamma 8:1).
he would not suffer even a little. He would not be willing to suffer even a little.
how is pain assessed where he took away a limb. And he has already paid him damage for the missing limb.
or to amputate it with a drug. Which removes the limb without pain.
and we assess how much difference there is between this and that. What is the difference between amputation by a sword and amputation by a drug.
loss of time. The cancellation of work caused by the injury.
like an idle laborer of that work from which he was idled. What payment he would accept in order not to engage in his work but to be idle.
and for loss of time we see him as if he were a cucumber watchman. For that is what he is fit for after the damage done to him, and therefore that is the work from which he is now considered idled.
cucumber watchman. Whose job is to walk beside the cucumbers.
a guard at the door. A person who watches the entrances of houses and courtyards and does not need to move.
blinded his eye. Blinded him.
makes him grind at the mill. Grinds at the millstones.

he gives him his full value, for he is not fit for work at all. And since he is completely idled from doing work, we value him as a slave sold in the market, how much he was worth before he was deafened, and he gives him this whole sum, and this is the payment of damage and loss of time together (Me'iri, Bava Kamma 85b; besides this he pays pain and shame, and the early authorities disagree whether he pays healing - see Rashi and Tosafot there).
he gives him his full value. And he does not give him the assessment value of each injury separately, which is higher than the assessment of his full value.

we collect from him only his full value. Since there is doubt here, we follow the rule that "the burden of proof is on the one who claims from his fellow," so that if the injured party wants to take the money from the damager, the burden of proving he is right is on him.

and if the injured party seized the damage of each and every limb and his full value. The separate assessment of each of the first three injuries together with the assessment of his full value after deducting the value of the first three injuries. And the sum of these assessments is higher than the assessment of his full value at once (Maggid Mishneh).

we do not take it from his hand. Although by strict law the damager is exempt, if the injured party already seized, we do not take it from his hand. For now he holds the money, and the damager who claims to be right must bring proof in order to take it from him.
he will live. He will recover.
and how much he needs. Each day for his medical needs.
to give a day's portion each day. To pay each day according to the assessment of that day.
and this is a benefit for the damager. So that he need not trouble himself with assessing and giving the medical needs each and every day.
he does not add anything to him. Even though in practice he lost work or the healing took longer than estimated.
for this is a benefit for him. And therefore he may waive it.
stipulate with me and give it into my hand. Give into my hand the sum allotted for the healing.
and I will establish myself as one of the known damagers. I will make for myself the name of a person established as a damager.
I will heal you. Even if he is a physician, for the injured party can claim that he does not take pleasure in being healed by the one who injured him (see Talmud Bava Kamma 85a and Rosh there 8:1).

I have a physician who heals for free, they do not listen to him. For the injured party can claim that a physician who receives no fee is not as careful in his work as one who is paid (Talmud, ibid.).
and growths arose on it. Pus or other growths formed in the wound or around it.
or the wound was opened again after it had healed. It reopened after it had recovered.
he must heal him and give him the value of his loss of time. For all this is a result of the damage he caused.

growths arose not because of the wound, he must heal him. From the words of the Talmud and the early authorities (Talmud Bava Kamma 85a) it emerges that for growths not caused by the wound he is exempt even from healing, and the commentators struggled to resolve the words of the Rambam. Some emended the text (Maggid Mishneh, Me'irat Einayim, R. Yosef Kapach), and some wrote various solutions (Kesef Mishneh, Merkevet HaMishneh, Yad Peshutah).
transgressed the physician's words. The physician's instructions.
and aggravated it. Made it worse.
he is not obligated to heal him. Since the injured party's negligence caused the aggravation of the illness.
and we do not fix a time for him at all. Unlike a loan, where the borrower is given thirty days to find money to repay the loan (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 22:1).
the lowly. A lowly person.
and turned its hem over his face. Raised the lower part of his garment.

one who shames a person who was made naked is not like one who shames one who is not naked. The payment for shame in these cases is less than for one who strips a fully clothed person, because he was not fully clothed before being shamed.
one who shames a sleeping person is liable for shame. For he will be shamed when he wakes.

and if he died in his sleep... we do not collect this shame from the one who shamed him. This payment is in doubt, whether he is exempt because he did not actually shame him or liable because of the shame of his family (see Talmud Bava Kamma 86b), and therefore we do not take money out of doubt.
and if the heirs seized, we do not take it from their hands. Like any monetary doubt (see above 2:13, Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:11).
one who shames a madman is exempt. Because shame does not apply to him at all.
and one who shames a deaf person is liable. Although he is not defined as having understanding for many matters, nevertheless if he is shamed he is hurt by it.
in any case one who shames a minor, etc., is not like.... For the shame of these is less.
with words. By speech.
or spat on his clothes, he is exempt. Since the spit did not touch his body, and one is not liable for shame until he does an act on the body of the one shamed (see Rosh, Bava Kamma 8:15).
and the court should fence in the matter everywhere and at all times as they see fit. The court should set a punishment for one who does these things in order to prevent such phenomena.
and if he shamed a Torah scholar he is liable to pay. As explained shortly.

for anyone who shames a Torah scholar, etc.. It is a great sin to disgrace the Sages and one who does so has no share in the World to Come, and in addition to the fine stated here he is liable to excommunication (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:11-12).
the weight of thirty-five gold dinars. Which is a litra of gold (below 5:6).
selas. A sela is four dinars (see below 5:10).

whether in the Land or outside the Land. Although the judges outside the Land (who are not ordained) have no authority to collect fines, not even those fines imposed by the Sages (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:8-9), the fine for shaming a Torah scholar is collected everywhere.
and so it is fitting for them. For the proper way for a Torah scholar is to forgive one who disgraces him (see Hilchot De'ot 5:13, Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:13).
but the judges would say to the one who shamed: you are obligated to give him a litra of gold. Because that is what he must pay by law, even though the Torah scholar may forgive it.
the rest of the people. One who is not a Torah scholar.
one who whitens a person's face. Whose fellow's face turns pale from shame.
and all of them are fines. For they are not assessed according to the results of the act.
and that fixed sum is the value of pain, shame, healing and loss of time. The fixed sum includes all four payments.
with his foot. With his foot.
with his knee. With his knee.
gathered his fingers as one binds a bundle. Made a fist.
struck his fellow with his palm. Hit him with the palm of his hand on one of the parts of his body.
slapped him on the face. Hit him with the palm of his hand on the face, and there is greater shame in this than in other parts of the body.
slapped him with the back of his hand. With the back of the hand, and there is greater shame in this than in a slap with the palm (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 8:6).
pinched his ear. Twisted and pinched it (ibid.).
who removed his cloak from upon him. Removed his upper garment from him.
who uncovered a woman's head. Removed her head covering so that her hair was revealed.

from the silver of the Land of Israel at that time, etc.. In the coin used at the time of this enactment there were seven parts copper and one part silver (see Hilchot Ishut 10:8), and since the sela is four dinars, half a dinar of this sela is silver and the rest copper (and these coins are called the "sela of the province").

he pays twelve and a half selas of pure silver. That is fifty silver dinars, the weight of the silver dinars found in a hundred selas of the silver of the time of the enactment, and likewise he must complete the value of three hundred fifty copper dinars (see Sma, Choshen Mishpat 420:60).
ugly ones. Whose conduct is ugly.
to take one perutah from the jesters who play with them. To earn a perutah from idle people who amuse themselves with them.

one who strikes a woman and her children come out, even though he did not intend. As in the case described in Scripture (Exodus 21:22), where during a quarrel between two men one pushed a pregnant woman in her belly without intending at all to injure or harm her, and as a result she miscarried and the offspring came out lifeless (see Responsa of the Rambam 353).

and damage and pain. Like the law of any injurer, who is liable for these payments because of the injury, and we estimate how much the woman's value decreased because of the miscarriage compared to the decrease in an ordinary birth, and this is the payment for damage, and how much pain she has from the miscarriage compared to the pain of an ordinary birth.

we assess the woman, how much she was worth before she gave birth, etc.. We estimate for how much she would have been sold in the market as a pregnant slave and for how much she would have been sold after giving birth (and we do not estimate the value of the offspring themselves, since in buying a pregnant woman there is a natural concern of miscarriage).
and if the husband died. After the striking.

they are given to his heirs. Although the offspring are part of the woman's body, the Torah gave the husband the value of the offspring, and if he was alive at the time of the striking he acquired it, and therefore the monetary right passes to his heirs.

and if he struck her after her husband's death, the value of the offspring also goes to the woman. In a case where the husband did not acquire them, the value of the offspring reverts to being part of the woman's body and belongs to her and not to her husband's heirs.

if the convert died, he is exempt. If he had no other children after he converted, so that he has no heirs to whom the monetary right to the value of the offspring would pass, and his law is like that of a debt with no claimants.
and if he injured her after the convert's death, she acquires the value of the offspring. Like the law of one who strikes a woman after her husband's death, as above, halakhah 2.
she was a maidservant or a gentile at the time of pregnancy. And at that time betrothal does not take effect on her.

the value of the offspring is hers. Even if at the time of the striking she was married to the husband, since at the time of pregnancy betrothal could not take effect on her, he is not considered her husband for the value of the offspring.
even though he was unintentional. He did not intend to kill her, and he is not liable to court-imposed death for this killing.
"and if there is no mishap, he shall surely be punished". This implies that if there is a mishap, he is not punished with payments.

Scripture did not distinguish between unintentional and deliberate in a matter that has court-imposed death to exempt him from payments. Scripture did not distinguish between a case where he struck the woman unintentionally and a case where he struck deliberately, and from this we learn that in every case where there was a mishap and the woman died, the striker is exempt from payments even if he is not actually liable to court-imposed death (see also Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:13).

where he intended the woman. That he intended to strike her but not to kill her, and since had he been deliberate he would have been liable to death, this act has a certain aspect of court-imposed death, and he is exempt from the payments.
but if he intended his fellow and struck the woman. Without intending to harm her at all.
this is like a matter that has no court-imposed death. For when it was done with no intention at all, there is no aspect of court-imposed death here and therefore he is not exempt from the payments.
a bruise. A blow that draws blood.
but if he made a bruise on them. And he is liable for this to court-imposed death by strangulation (Hilchot Mamrim 5:5).

or he injured his fellow on Shabbat. And he is liable to court-imposed death like a Shabbat violator, for injuring is included in the labor of tearing, which is a derivative of threshing (Hilchot Shabbat 8:7).
and we have already explained. Above, halakhah 5.
and all who ruin on Shabbat are exempt from death. For one of the conditions for liability to death for doing a labor on Shabbat is that it be constructive and not destructive (Hilchot Shabbat 1:17).
since he gave satisfaction to his evil inclination at the time he injured his fellow. For through the striking his mind was cooled and his anger calmed (ibid. 8:8).
he is like one who repairs. And one who ruins in order to repair is liable (ibid. 1:18).

one who injures his fellow on Yom Kippur, even deliberately, is liable for payments. For one who does work on Yom Kippur is not liable to court-imposed death but to karet, and liability to karet does not exempt from payments (see Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:11, Hilchot Genevah 3:2).
but does not everyone liable to lashes and payments receive lashes and not pay. See also Hilchot Na'arah Betulah, ibid., Hilchot Genevah 3:1.
so it is in everything except one who injures his fellow. See below 5:3, that even with an injurer there is a case where he is flogged and does not pay.
one who injures his own Canaanite slave is exempt. Because everything this slave acquires belongs to his master, these payments in any case belong to his master.
one who injures his own Hebrew slave is liable for all of them except loss of time. Since he stands in his own domain and only his labor belongs to his master, he is exempt only from loss of time.

and even if he pained him with a drug and he healed quickly. Even if his master used a caustic drug to hasten his recovery and did not spend all of the healing payment, the surplus does not go to the slave for the pain he suffered, but to the master.

any slave who went out to freedom and the writ of release has not yet reached his hand. A Canaanite slave whose law is to go free but who has not yet been given the writ of release, for example the master declared him ownerless (Hilchot Avadim 8:13) or took from him one of his main limbs (ibid. 5:4).

has no fine. The law of the fine for slaves does not apply to him. For if this slave was gored by an ox and died, the owner of the ox is not obligated to pay the master the fine, because the slave is considered one who has no master (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 11:1).

he cannot take from them for himself, for his release is not yet complete. Since the process of his release is not finished, his status is in doubt, and therefore he cannot take money from the injurer out of doubt.
nor can the master take from them, for he has no ownership left in him. Since the slave is considered one who has no master, his master too cannot collect the payments.
therefore one who knocks out his slave's tooth. And the slave thereby goes free but still needs a writ of release.

and if he seized, we do not take it from his hand. Like any monetary doubt in which we do not take money from the one holding it (see also above 3:3; and in Hilchot Avadim 5:14 it implies that in any case he gives him the value of his eye, see the commentary there).

one who is half slave and half free. For example, two partners one of whom freed his share in the slave (see Hilchot Avadim 7:4), and his law is that one day he works for the master and one day for himself. And although the law is that his master is compelled to free him (ibid. 7:7), he is not considered one whose release is delayed, for as long as his master has not freed him in practice he is not freed at all (Me'iri, Gittin 42b; and see Ra'avad, Lechem Mishneh and Me'irat Einayim).
if it happened to him, etc.. He gives the payment to whoever is entitled to the work of his hands on that day.

is liable for five things and land is bought with them. He must pay the slave all five payments, for the body of the Hebrew slave is not owned by his master, and the land bought with these payments belongs to the slave (but with the healing payment he does not buy land, since the slave is healed with it - Maggid Mishneh).

and his master eats its produce. Because this is damage that hinders the slave's work and harms his abilities, the master eats the produce in compensation for the decrease in his slave's work value due to the injury.
and his master has no produce from them. For the slave's work was not damaged by this injury.
a minor. One who has not yet completed twelve full years (Hilchot Ishut 2:1).
one who reduces her from her price. Who reduces her value if she were sold as a maidservant.

for the work of her hands and the money of her sale belong to her father. A father is entitled to the work of his daughter's hands until she comes of age (see Hilchot Ishut 3:11), and therefore the loss of time payment belongs to him; likewise he may sell his minor daughter as a maidservant (see Hilchot Avadim 4:1), and therefore the damage payment for reducing her value belongs to him.

and likewise damage that does not reduce her from her price is hers. For the father has no connection to this type of damage which does not reduce her value (and the commentators discussed which damage does not reduce her value - see Or Sameach and Yad Peshutah).
and likewise one who injures his daughter pays her pain, healing and shame. But the payments of damage and loss of time belong to him.

loss of time and healing go to her husband. Loss of time because the work of her hands is his, and healing because in any case the husband's duty is to heal his wife (Hilchot Ishut 12:2), and therefore he heals her and receives the healing payment from the injurer.

and shame and damage, etc.. The payments of shame and damage are shared by both, because the husband too is ashamed by his wife's shame and is harmed by her being blemished. But in the case of an injury in a hidden place the husband is harmed little by it and therefore receives one third, and when the injury is in a visible place the husband is harmed more and therefore receives two thirds of the payment.

and the wife's portion is used to buy land and the husband eats the produce. Like the law of property that came to the wife after marriage ("plucked property" - Hilchot Ishut 16:2), which belongs to the wife while the husband enjoys the profits of this property (see ibid. 22:21-22).
he must pay her all the damage and pain and all the shame. And he also heals her, as explained shortly, but he does not pay loss of time, for the work of her hands is his.
and the husband has no produce from them. For the Sages fined the husband so that he not benefit from the damage he caused (Kesef Mishneh, based on the Tur in the name of the Geonim).
and in this. In this way.
and the husband heals her as he heals any illness of hers. As part of the husband's obligations toward his wife.
and one who damages his wife during marital relations. While engaged in marital relations.
is liable for her damages. Although he did not intend to damage, nevertheless he is liable to pay because he should have been careful (see Talmud Bava Kamma 32a).
an addition to her ketubah. A sum he committed to pay her beyond the basic ketubah amount that he owes.

we compel her to sell the addition to her husband for the value of benefit. The value of benefit is the payment for the chance to collect her ketubah addition if she is divorced or widowed, and since the woman may die before that and the ketubah would not come to collection, the value of the benefit is lower than the amount of the ketubah addition itself. She sells the benefit to her husband, and collects the five payments from the sale price.
and if he wishes to divorce her, etc.. In which case he is obligated to pay her the ketubah and its addition, and he deducts the injury payment from the payment.
for it is forbidden for a person, etc.. Hilchot Ishut 10:10.
we write a document against her for the value of her injury. A promissory note for the amount of the injury, to be collected when she has property that is solely in her possession.

land is bought for them with their damage and they eat its produce. Since they do not know how to guard their money, land is bought with the payments and its profit is theirs, and when they grow up they will decide for themselves what to do with the land.

and if they were supported at his table and he injured them, he is exempt. For a father may strike his children for their education (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 5:6), and sometimes he strikes his children more than is proper, and if we held him liable for payments this could cause enmity between him and his children and he would not let them be supported at his table (Ramban, Milchamot HaShem, Bava Kamma 31a).

and if others injured them, etc.. Although the findings of children supported at their father's table belong to the father to prevent enmity (see Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:13 and the commentary there), the law of damage payments is different since they come because of pain, and therefore the father is not particular about them and they belong to the children (see Talmud Bava Kamma 87b).
if they are not supported at his table. If they are not sustained by him.
and the minors. Who are not supported at his table.

and they who injured others are exempt. And the Rambam wrote regarding those mentioned here and in the previous halakhah: "But the judge may strike them severely to prevent damage to people" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 8:4, and see also Hilchot Genevah 1:10).

but they pay later if the woman is divorced or her husband dies. And in this case we do not sell her ketubah for the value of benefit to pay for the injury (for the reason see Talmud Bava Kamma 89a-b).
like a debtor who has nothing with which to pay. Who has no money to pay his debt.
exempt from payments. Because the slave could have removed the coal or come up out of the sea or the fire, so it turns out the slave caused himself to die.
and if he did so to his fellow's animal he is liable. Since it does not know how to save itself.

whether himself or his fellow. And there is a difference between them, for the prohibition of striking one's fellow is explicit in the Torah (as explained shortly), whereas the prohibition of striking oneself is not explicit and is learned from the Sages' interpretation (see Talmud Bava Kamma 91b; and see Hilchot Shevuot 5:16-17 and the commentary there).
and not only the injurer but anyone who strikes. The liability is not only for making a wound, which is a blow that draws blood, but for any blow.
in the manner of a quarrel. In the course of a fight.
transgresses a negative commandment. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 16:12.
as it is said, "he shall not add... to strike him". This verse was said regarding the striking of sinners liable to lashes.
for there are no payments here, etc.. Usually, an injurer is exempt from lashes because he pays (as above 4:9), and since in this case there is no obligation of payment, he is flogged.

and even if he struck his fellow's slave. A Canaanite slave, for whose injury the injurer owes the master five payments (as above 4:10); in a case where there is no obligation of payment, he is flogged.

and a gentile who struck an Israelite is liable to death. Even for a blow worth less than a perutah. But he is not put to death by the court; rather he is liable to death at the hands of Heaven (see Hilchot Melachim 10:6).
by taking an object. While holding a Torah scroll in his hand (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
this injury. This wound.
into his hand. Into his domain or his place.
and they did not see him at the time he injured him. But only when he entered and left.
in what case is this said. That he must swear in order to take.
in a place where he could strike it himself. Where the injured party could cause this injury to himself.

for there was a third person with them, and it is possible that this injured party told him to injure him and blame another. Besides the injured party and the defendant there was another person, and perhaps the injured party asked him to injure him in order to place the blame on the defendant.
he takes without an oath. Since it is certain that this person struck him.

the injurer admitted that he injured, he pays five things, for the witnesses were there, etc.. Although there is an admission here, and he should be exempt from damage and pain like one who admits to a fine (see the next halakhah), since the main liability is based on the witnesses, he is liable for everything (R. Yosef ibn Migash, Shevuot 46b).
and is liable for loss of time, shame and healing on his own admission. For these payments are not fines but money, as explained in the next halakhah.

swears the oath of heset. When the defendant denies everything, although by Torah law he need not swear, the Sages imposed an obligation of an oath on him (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:2-3). And although one does not swear the oath of heset on a matter for which one who admits is exempt from paying (ibid. 1:15), in this case he swears since he pays loss of time, shame and healing on his own admission.
and shame. For which he is liable even though it does not reduce the injured party's property.
and his admission in court is what shamed him. So that there is no admission here regarding the shame; rather the shame itself is caused by the admission, and the court are the witnesses to it.

for one who damages his fellow's property, once he has paid what he is liable to pay, is atoned for. What he sinned against his fellow, but he must repent for this, confess and accept upon himself never to do so again (see Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1).
five things. The five types of payments.
rams of Nebaioth. An expression for choice offerings (based on Isaiah 60:7).
until he asks the injured party and he forgives him. And see Hilchot Teshuvah 2:9 for what he should do if he did not forgive him.
and it is forbidden for the injured party to be cruel, etc.. See also Hilchot De'ot 6:6, Hilchot Teshuvah 2:10.
he is liable to pay even though he permitted him to destroy. Since he did not explicitly exempt him.

when the vessels came into his hand first as a guard... he is liable to pay. Since they were given to him to guard them and that is his role, it is not enough that the owner of the vessels told him to break them.
he is liable to pay. The one who breaks, and the one who sent him is not liable.
for he caused a blind person to stumble, etc.. And he transgressed the command "and before the blind you shall not put a stumbling block" (see Hilchot Rotze'ach UShemirat Nefesh 12:14).
he must pay full damage. And pays from the best of his property (above 1:11).
whether he was unintentional or compelled. Even asleep, for a person is always forewarned against damaging (ibid.).
everything is one law. For all are included in one who damages his fellow's property, and the animal is mentioned only as an example.
both were with permission. For example, the homeowner gave the damager permission to enter, or they were in the public domain where both have permission to walk.
or both without permission. For example, they entered another person's courtyard without his permission.
and one of them damaged his fellow's property unintentionally, he is exempt. Unless he deviated from the usual conduct in that place, in which case he is liable (as below, halakhot 8-9).
a rung. The rung of a ladder.

and if it was strong and fastened and it slipped out or became worm-eaten. For the rung appeared strong and fastened, but it slipped out unexpectedly or became worm-eaten inside and this could not be noticed from outside (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 12:5).
for this is a blow from Heaven. For it does not depend on him and could not be foreseen and avoided (compare ibid. 14:2).
as we explained. Above, halakhah 3.
he is exempt for them. For one who damages in his own domain is not liable unless he intended to damage deliberately (as above, halakhah 3).
on top of his fellow. On top of another ox.
whether it was innocuous. Whether the upper ox was innocuous, in which case, if it had indeed damaged, its owner would pay half damage to the owner of the lower ox.

or whether it was forewarned... he is exempt. Even though if the upper ox was forewarned, its owner is liable for full damage for the damage it did, nevertheless the owner of the lower ox may let his ox slip away in order to save it and to avoid the trouble of claiming the damage. For a person has the right to save his property from damage, and whenever he does so carefully so as not to damage his fellow's property, he is exempt (and for this reason he is exempt even if the oxen were in the public domain or in the domain of the injured party - Yad Peshutah).
if he could have let it slip away. If he could have let the lower ox slip away instead of pushing the upper ox and causing it damage.

he is liable. For he has no right to cause damage that is not necessary, and even when it happened in his own domain he is liable because he could have saved his property without causing the damage and is considered to have intended to damage.
two who were walking in the public domain. Facing each other.
this one comes with his barrel and this one comes with his beam. One carries a barrel and the other carries a beam.
for this one has permission to walk and this one has permission to walk. And it is considered as though he damaged in the domain of both (as above, halakhah 3).
and the barrel carrier was last. Behind the beam carrier.
and the barrel broke on the beam, he is exempt. For the barrel carrier ran into the beam and caused damage to himself.

and if the beam carrier stopped to rest from the weight of his load, he is liable. For sudden rest without prior notice is considered a deviation from the usual way of carrying loads in the public domain. And since the injured party has permission to walk and the damager has no permission to behave this way, it is as though he damaged in the injured party's domain, where one is liable even without intent (Arukh HaShulchan 379:3).
and if the barrel carrier warned, etc.. The beam carrier warned the barrel carrier and cried out that he was stopping and told him to halt, and the other continued and the barrel broke.
he stopped to adjust his load. He stopped to arrange the load on him.
for he is busy on his way. And there is no deviation here from the usual way of carrying loads in the public domain.

he is liable, for this is as if he broke it with his hand deliberately. For it is his responsibility to carry the beam so that it does not damage, and if he did not, he is considered negligent and as one who damaged intentionally.
and if the barrel carrier stopped to rest, he is exempt. The beam carrier.
and if the beam carrier warned. The barrel carrier warned the beam carrier.
and if he stopped to adjust his load, even if he did not warn the beam carrier, he is liable. For the barrel carrier did not deviate from the usual way.
and likewise this one comes with his lamp and this one with his flax. And the flax was set on fire by the lamp.

because he runs with permission so that Shabbat not enter while he is not free. For he is hurrying to finish his preparations for Shabbat in order to complete his tasks and be free to receive Shabbat.
and they injured each other, both are exempt. For both deviated from the usual conduct in the public domain.
who released water. Opened a flow of water by removing what was blocking it.
who spat or blew his nose. Expelled fluids from the body by spitting or coughing and the like.
with his force and his mucus. Types of phlegm expelled from the body.

this is like one who damages with his hand, and these are derivatives of a person. Damage that comes from a person's force is considered to come from him directly, and its law is the same as that of one who damaged with his hand (similar to property damage whose derivatives are like the primary categories - see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:10).

he is liable on account of his pit. Which is one of the primary categories of damages in property damage, and its liability rules differ from the laws of a person who damages (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 13:1, and see below, halakhah 16).
as we explained. Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 13:2.
a polisher. A craftsman who prepares and sharpens iron tools.
a spark. A spark of fire.
to demolish it. To take it apart.
and broke the stones. Instead of taking the wall apart without breaking the stones.
or damaged. Something else by demolishing the wall.

he was demolishing from one side and it fell from another side, he is exempt. For this fall was not caused by his action, but the wall weakened from his blows and the stones' joining loosened and the stone fell by its own weight, and therefore this damage is not attributed to him and he is exempt.
and if because of the blow he is liable. If the other side fell by the force of his blow, since this blow came from his force he is liable (see below 7:7).
one who pressed his fellow's animal into the water. Pressed the animal and lowered it below the surface of the water.

or placed it in the sun and confined the place around it. Limited its movement to the place where the sun is. But if he placed it unable to move in a shaded place where the sun was going to come and kill it, he is exempt by human law (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 3:9-11, and see there further cases belonging to this law).
they divide among themselves. They divide the payment among themselves (as above 1:13).
and once this one added his bundle it stood and did not move. And afterwards it died, and therefore the last one is liable, for his bundle caused the animal's death.
and if it was not walking from the beginning, the last is exempt. Since even without his placing it, it would have died.
and if it is not known. It is not known whether it was walking before he placed the last bundle.

all pay equally. For all were negligent, since each of them had the duty to ensure that the animal was not loaded with a burden beyond its strength (Yad Peshutah, and see Ketzot HaChoshen 383:1, who explained otherwise).
even though it was fit to break under them before he sat. For if they had continued to sit on it, it would eventually have broken even without the last one.
for we say to him. They can claim against him.
all of them are liable. And they divide the payment among themselves.
a person and an ox that pushed. Together.
an animal of disqualified sacrificial animals. An animal that was consecrated for a sacrifice and became disqualified (for example, a blemish fell in it) and whose law is to be redeemed.
into a pit. The owner of the pit is liable for its damages (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 12:1-2).

and the one pushed was injured, etc.. So that there are three causes of the damage - the person, the ox and the pit - and each has different liability rules in the different types of damages, as will be explained.

regarding damages to a person or damage to an animal. Regarding liability for damage caused to the person or animal that was pushed, all the damagers are liable, and therefore they divide the damage payment among them.

regarding the value of offspring and the four things. If they pushed a pregnant woman and she miscarried, payment of the value of the offspring falls only on the person, for the Torah imposed the value of offspring only on a person (ibid. 11:3). And likewise the law regarding the four payments that accompany damage (pain, healing, loss of time, shame), which also apply only to a person who injures his fellow (ibid. 7:3).

regarding ransom. In a case where the one pushed was killed, the owner of the ox alone is obligated to pay the ransom (which is the value of the one killed according to the judges' assessment), as an owner of an ox that killed a person pays (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 10:2).
and thirty of a slave. Thirty silver selas, the fixed ransom value that the owner of an ox that killed another person's Canaanite slave pays (ibid. 11:1).

and the person and the owner of the pit are exempt. For a person who murdered does not pay ransom (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 1:4), and the owner of the pit is exempt since for a pit he is liable only if the person who fell into it was injured and not if he died (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 12:16).

regarding vessels and disqualified sacrificial animals... and the owner of the pit is exempt. For on the liability of pit damages one is not liable for damage caused to vessels (ibid. 13:1), nor for the death of a disqualified sacrificial animal (ibid. 12:17).
one who made his fellow's pure food impure. For example, he was impure with corpse impurity and touched pure food belonging to his fellow and made it impure.

or who mixed his produce with terumah. Mixed terumah produce into his fellow's ordinary produce, and the ordinary produce does not have a ratio of a hundred to the terumah, and from now on all the produce has the law of terumah that is permitted to eat only to priests, and therefore the value of the produce dropped (see Hilchot Terumot 13:2).

or mixed a drop of libation wine into his wine. Wine that was poured as a libation to idolatry is not nullified in a mixture but forbids it in any amount, and the entire mixture is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'akhalot Assurot 15:6-7).
from the best of his property, as is the way of all damagers. See below, halakhah 16.
for the Sages fined only the one who transgressed and damaged, but the heir who did nothing they did not fine. For this principle see Hilchot Yom Tov 7:4, Hilchot Bechorot 2:7 and elsewhere.
for they fined only one who intended to damage knowingly. For only for the deliberate does the reason apply that everyone not go around damaging his fellow.

the priests who made the sacrifice piggul. Disqualified the offering at the time of its slaughter or the sprinkling of its blood by an intention that disqualifies (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 13:1).
are liable to pay. The owner of the offering the value of the offering that was disqualified, although it is damage that is not visible.

and likewise one who does work with a sin offering cow. A red heifer designated to purify those impure through contact with the dead, which is disqualified if work was done with it (Hilchot Parah Adumah 1:7).
and with the waters of the sin offering. Water designated for sprinkling on those impure through contact with the dead to purify them, which is disqualified if work was done with it (ibid. 7:1).
deliberately he is liable to pay. The value of the cow or the water, even though it is damage that is not visible.
brought in a cow. A red heifer that was not his.
to the fattening place. A place where calves are fattened.

so that it nurse and thresh. For the sake of nursing a calf and threshing grain. And threshing is a labor that disqualifies it, and even if it threshed on its own, since he brought it in with the intention that it thresh, it is disqualified by this (see Hilchot Parah Adumah 1:7). [Note: some versions read: "that it nurse."]

and diverted his attention from the waters of the sin offering. Or he weighed sin offering waters and during the weighing diverted his attention from them, and they are disqualified by this (ibid. 10:5).
exempt by human law. Although he disqualified them, we do not hold him liable in court because in these cases he did no act on the body of the thing damaged.
and liable by the laws of Heaven. Morally he is responsible for what happened and should pay (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 2:19 and the rulings and opinions there).
for no Israelite forbids something that is not his. Because his intention is not to pour a libation to idolatry but to distress his fellow (see Talmud Chullin 41a, Hilchot Shechitah 2:21).

and if he had a partnership in it or was an apostate, etc.. In these cases we do not say that he intended to distress his fellow but to pour the wine as a libation, and therefore the wine becomes forbidden and he must pay his fellow for this damage, although it is damage that is not visible.

or they warned him and he accepted the warning, for he is an apostate. For it is evident that he commits the transgression to spite, and he is an apostate for one transgression, who is treated as an apostate for the entire Torah (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:9).

and how can this one be liable to pay when he is liable with his life. For one who pours a libation to idolatry is liable to death (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 3:3), and one liable to death and money for one act is exempt from the payments (as above 4:5).

because from the time that he lifted it, etc.. The exemption from payment applies only if the liability to death and to money were simultaneous, but if they were at different times during the same act, he is not exempt from paying (see Hilchot Genevah 3:1-2). In the case stated here, the monetary liability was already at the stage of lifting, and the liability to death was only at the time of the actual libation, and therefore he pays.
anyone who causes damage to his fellow's property is liable to pay. See also Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 14:7.
even though he is not the one who damages, this very damage in the end, etc.. Although the final act of damage was not done by him, since he is the cause of it, he is liable (as below, halakhah 8).
on cushions and pillows. And had the vessels fallen on them they would not have broken.

he is liable for full damage. The remover is liable to pay all the damage. And the owner of the vessel is not defined as a partner in the damage, because when throwing he thought that the cushions and pillows were in place, and it would not have occurred to him that someone would remove them from there (Derishah, Choshen Mishpat 386).

and the owner of the vessel went first and removed the cushions, the thrower is liable. And he is liable to pay all the damage, because a person has no right to throw a vessel that is not his onto cushions and pillows that are not his on the assumption that they will not be removed, and the owner of the cushions and pillows is not considered a partner in the damage because he has the right to remove them whenever he wishes (Derishah, Choshen Mishpat 386).
and likewise one who burns his fellow's documents. Promissory notes, so that he can now not collect his debt.
for although the document itself is not money. And he did not damage actual money.

for it is a validated document. Whose signatures were confirmed by the court as valid signatures. For if not, one cannot collect with this document, since one can claim that the signatures were forged.
and so it was written in it. That the burner admits that the sum the owner of the documents claims was indeed written in them.

and it is because he burned it that he cannot collect the debt. For had it not been for the act of burning, the debt could have been collected. But if he lent to a violent or poor person and the document could not be collected in any case, or the lender forgave the debt and the like, the damager is exempt (Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Kamma 98b).
but if he did not believe him. And the injured party has no proof for his claim.
Reuben who was owed by Simeon. Simeon owed him money.
and sold the document to Levi. Reuben sold Levi the promissory note and the right to collect the debt from Simeon.

Simeon is released, as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Mechirah 6:12. For although by rabbinic enactment the debt and the lien in the document can be sold, this sale is not effective by Torah law, and therefore the lender can forgive the debt and his forgiveness takes effect. So when Reuben forgave Simeon his debt, the document he sold to Levi became worthless, and he lost the value of the debt.
and likewise if Reuben's heir forgave him, etc.. For even the heir of the creditor can forgive the debt even if the promissory note was sold to another (ibid.).

and likewise one who makes his slave a security. Who owed a debt to his fellow, and designated the slave for collection of the debt, for example he stipulated that the lender would collect his debt only from the slave and not from the borrower's other property (Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 4:4, Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 18:6).
and then freed him. After pledging the slave for payment of the debt, the borrower went and freed the slave, and the law is that his freeing cancels the lender's lien and the slave goes free.

and we compel the debtor too to free the slave, so that he not meet him and say to him: you are my slave. Although the freeing cancels the lien and the slave is defined as freed, for the sake of the world's order we compel the lender to free him so that he not claim that he is his slave by virtue of the lien (ibid.).

and likewise one who pushes his fellow's coin and it rolled and went down to the sea. And he did not damage the coin itself, for it is in the sea intact, and the damage caused to its owner is that he cannot reach the coin.
and likewise one that is perforated. Pierced; this blemish disqualifies it from being offered or from serving as a red heifer (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 7:3, Hilchot Parah Adumah 1:7).
one who beats out. Flattens, spreads thin.
and removed their image. He removed the image engraved on them, and as a result they lost their value, for they are no longer coins but pieces of metal.
the other is exempt. And the one who threw is liable, for his throwing is the first cause of the breaking of the vessel (as above, halachah 8).

an ox that was slated for execution because it damages people. For example, one that was grazing in fields and vineyards and is slated for execution because of this damage (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:1), or that killed a person and is slated for execution (Meiri, Bava Kamma 91b; and see Yeshuot Shlomo ibid. 8:60, that this refers to the present time, when courts do not judge such cases and its execution falls on its owner).
and a tree that is slated for cutting down because it endangers the public. For example, where there is concern that it will fall into the public domain (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 13:19).
as the judges see fit. According to what the judges determine.

for he has prevented them from performing a commandment. For by law one is obligated to remove the hazard, and it is a commandment to heed the words of the Sages (Rabbeinu Chananel, Bava Kamma 91b), or it is on account of the commandment "do not place blood in your house" (Yeshuot Shlomo, and see Hilchot Rotze'ach U'Shemirat Nefesh 11:4).
since it was slated for this, he is exempt. For then the claim of the damager has substance, and it is reasonable that the owner indeed said so to him.
and likewise one who slaughtered a wild animal or bird and another came and covered the blood. He fulfilled the commandment of covering the blood with earth in its place (see Hilchot Shechitah 14:1).

they assess for the one who damaged by his own hand just as they assess for him if his property damaged. The manner of assessing the damage and the obligation to pay of one who damages his fellow himself is the same as that of one whose property damaged his fellow.

and he pays the depreciation to the injured party together with the carcass or the broken vessel. He gives the injured party the carcass of his animal or his broken vessel, and makes up the difference between their present value and their original value.
in the way we explained regarding his ox that damaged. Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 7:8-9.
one who trod his fellow's grapes, they assess his damage for him. He made wine of them and caused a loss, for example it spoiled or lost value.

when the depreciation is collected from the damager, it is collected from his movable property. And even if the movable property he has is the waste of grain after milling ("bran"), it takes precedence in collection over land (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 8:10).
from the best of his property. The best land he owns (ibid.).
anyone who damages his fellow's property and does not know what he damaged. The damager does not know what he damaged, so that we could estimate how much he must pay.

the injured party swears by the enactment of the Sages and collects. By Torah law the claimant must prove his claim and is not believed on his oath. But the Sages penalized the damager to pay after the injured party swears how much was damaged by him.

like the robbed party. For regarding him too they enacted that he swears against the robber and collects from him (Hilchot Gezelah 4:1). The reason for these enactments is "so that damages and lawlessness among people will not multiply" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 7:3).
provided that he claims things that he is presumed to have, as we explained regarding the robbed party. Hilchot Gezelah 4:3, that he claims items that it is reasonable to say were in his possession.
a purse. A wallet.
or he handed it over to a coercer and it was lost. That he showed a person who takes property by force his fellow's purse, and he took it (see below 8:1).

swears while holding an object. He swears how many gold coins were in the wallet, while holding a Torah scroll in his hand (see Hilchot Shevuot 11:8), by the law of those who swear and collect (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:2).
things that he is presumed to have or presumed to have deposited with him. That it is reasonable to say that the claimant owned such items or that they were deposited with him for safekeeping.
and it is their way to be placed in a purse. For items of this kind are usually placed in a wallet.

but if it is not their way to be placed in this vessel, he was negligent against himself. He caused himself damage, for even if he is telling the truth he cannot take them on his oath (Maggid Mishneh, and see Piskei VeShitot).
a wineskin. A flask, a small leather bag.
and covered. Covered over.

and if he seized, they do not remove it from his hand, etc.. Because in this case it is in doubt whether the oath of the injured party is effective, if he seized, they do not remove it from his hand, like any monetary doubt (see also above 2:13).

for this damager is obligated to swear and cannot swear. The damager is obligated to swear by Torah law like one who admits part of a claim, but because he does not know how many gold coins were there, he cannot swear and pays according to the claim of the injured party.
as will be explained regarding the deposit. Hilchot She'elah U'Pikadon 5:6.
coercer. A person who takes property by force.
is obligated to pay from the best of his property. By the law of a damager (above 7:16).

and if he died, it is collected from his heirs like all other damagers. By the law of any damager who died before paying (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 8:11-12). For this payment is a full monetary obligation, and is not defined as a fine, whose liability does not pass to heirs (Maggid Mishneh, and see above 7:3).

even though the informer did not carry it and did not put it in his hand but only caused it. The informer's liability applies not only where he took the money in his own hands from the injured party and brought it to the coercer, but also if he caused the coercer to take his fellow's money, for example by showing him his money and the like.
caused. Caused an action to be done (compare Hilchot Bekhorot 2:8).
for one who saves himself with his fellow's money must pay. Below, halachah 13.
storehouse. A stockpile.
and an informer stood up. On his own.
or until he shows him the property of so-and-so who is fleeing from him. The property of a person who escaped from the king.
he is exempt, etc.. Since he did not damage with his hands, and he is not obligated to remain silent and put himself in danger so that his fellow's money will not be damaged.

and even if this informer who showed it carried it. For what he showed he is not liable because he was coerced and he did not carry or give by hand. And for carrying the money by hand afterward he is not liable because at that time the money was already considered lost.
as if it were burned. And when he carries and gives by hand he does not damage his fellow.
and remove the hand of the coercer from between them. He will make sure that the gentiles release the land or the movable property.
and they shall go to judgment among Israel. They shall go to a Jewish court, which will decide their dispute.
one who was seized on account of his fellow and gentiles took money from him because of his fellow. That they took money from him on the pretext that they could not get his fellow.
his fellow is not obligated to pay. And he is not considered one who saves himself with his fellow's money.

and there is no one seized on account of his fellow ... except one seized on account of the tax, etc.. Since the tax and the tribute are personal and are also taken lawfully (Maggid Mishneh, Mirkevet HaMishneh), they fall on his fellow, and his fellow has the law of one who saves himself with his fellow's money.
the tribute. A gift that one is obligated to give.
provided that they took it from him explicitly on account of so-and-so before witnesses. For he must prove that he paid on behalf of his fellow.

and the witnesses do not know how much he lost him ... if the informed-upon one seized, they do not remove it from his hand. In this case it is in doubt whether the informed-upon party swears and collects as was enacted for the robbed party (Hilchot Gezelah 4:1) or not. Therefore the court does not obligate on the basis of the informed-upon party's oath, but if the informed-upon party seized the informer's property, they do not remove it from his hand, and he swears how much was taken from him and accordingly they leave it with him.
but swears while holding an object. While holding a Torah scroll in his hand (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
with clear proof. By the testimony of valid witnesses who will testify clearly how much money they lost through the informing.

a severe oath. An oath that judges administer to one who is obligated to swear by Torah law or by rabbinic law, taken while holding an object. For example, where there is one witness to the informing, and one witness obligates an oath by Torah law.

the oath of hesset. A lighter oath, enacted by the Sages of the Talmud, without holding an object, which everyone who denies his fellow's claim must take (see Hilchot Shevuot 11:7-8 and ibid. halachah 13). For example, where there are no witnesses to the informing but only a claim.
because he is wicked, and there is none more disqualified than this. Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 2:2.
he is not wicked, but only subject to payment. Because he was coerced; a monetary debt rests on him but his status regarding oaths does not change.
even if he oppressed and afflicted him. But if he oppresses and afflicts the public, it is permitted to inform on him (below, halachah 11).
he has no share in the World to Come. Hilchot Teshuvah 3:6.

it is permitted to kill the informer anywhere, even at the present time when capital cases are not judged. Even where there are no ordained judges, or nowadays when there is no ordination and capital cases are not judged. The reason is that killing him is not an act of punishment that must be done by a court but an act of rescue and prevention of loss, because gentiles have no mercy on one who falls into their hands, and the informer endangers the life of the one informed upon.
light money. Of low value.
he has made himself liable to death. He brought himself to a state in which it is permitted to kill him.
it is a commandment to kill him. Just as it is a commandment to save the pursued from the hand of his pursuer who wants to kill him (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 1:6 ff.).
in the cities of the West. Spain or North Africa.
according to their wickedness. In keeping with the severity of their deeds.

or to commit a transgression. To commit a transgression of forbidden relations against him, for example, he chased a betrothed girl to rape her (see Hilchot Rotze'ach 1:10-11); in all these cases the law is that it is a commandment to kill the pursuer.

because he is liable with his life. For during the pursuit it is permitted to kill him as one liable to death, and one is not liable to pay money for an act for which one is liable to death (see Hilchot Genevah 3:1, 9:13).
his money shall not be dearer than his body. If it is permitted to kill the pursuer in order to be saved from him, all the more so is it permitted to break his vessels.
for one who saves himself with his fellow's money is liable. See also above 5:2.
and not by law. For by law he is liable if he broke others' vessels.
but an enactment. An enactment of the Sages.
or he should delay and consider at the time when he pursues. He should be careful not to damage others and delay saving the pursued.
and one of them stood up and lightened the load. See Hilchot Gezelah 12:14 on how the loss is divided among the owners of the load (and see further Aruch HaShulchan 380:8).
